title: Google DeepMind Agent Teams Discover Lean-Verified Quantum Algorithms
html:
Key PointsLean verification lets agents optimize circuits beyond what classical simulation can…
View more

  • Lean verification lets agents optimize circuits beyond what classical simulation can test.
  • Fusion simulation cost fell 11.8-fold through a real-space grid and momentum register.
  • Reported gains remain bounded by specifications that exclude error correction and routing.

Google DeepMind presented research on November 23, 2026 showing that teams of Gemini 4 agents, checked by the Lean theorem prover, produced lower-cost quantum programs for five problems. Its largest scientific gain was an 11.8-fold reduction in the estimated cost of a fusion simulation, in work with Google Quantum AI.

The work covered parallel Grover search, fixed-point arcsin arithmetic and three simulations: alpha-particle stopping power in fusion fuel, non-Born–Oppenheimer molecular dynamics and Cytochrome P450 energy estimation. For fault-tolerant circuits, researchers measured spacetime cost as peak logical qubits multiplied by T-gate count, combining memory demand with operations that are costly in error-corrected quantum computers.

Proof Checking Expands the Search Space

Quantum algorithm discovery has an evaluation problem: candidates spanning hundreds or thousands of qubits generally cannot be tested through classical simulation or on present quantum processors. DeepMind’s system therefore treats a proposed circuit as a mathematical object. Researchers wrote frozen Lean specifications containing correctness and resource-cost theorems; agents supplied programs, cost bounds and proofs, using high-level optimization prompts rather than problem-specific starting ideas. The large autonomous runs used Gemini 4 Carbon models.

The Lean 4 library is grounded in quantum Hoare logic, a logic for reasoning about preconditions and postconditions, and handles classical control flow alongside unitary operations, measurement and qubit reset. It can prove bounds on expected or worst-case resource costs. An external verifier replayed every submission in a clean sandbox against the frozen specification, checking dependent definitions, permitted axioms and claimed costs to prevent agents from weakening theorems or otherwise gaming local checks.

Independent teams shared their best verified solutions, reusable lemmas and reviewed dead-end notes through a wiki, while agents met every four hours in virtual conferences to critique proposals. Conference claims counted only after verification. The paper estimates that, averaged across the three scientific applications, 61% of the measured cost reduction originated within teams, 15% came through cross-team wiki material and 24% through conferences, while cautioning that credit is difficult to separate cleanly.

What the Agents Changed

For fusion stopping power, the discovered circuit moves electron interactions onto a real-space grid and uses Pauli exclusion to simplify short-range interactions. The paper reports that this cut walk steps by a factor of 12.8; retaining total electron momentum in a 42-qubit register reduced T gates per step by another 10%. The resulting circuit needs 4,338 logical qubits, down from 5,650, but uses 1.42 times as many T gates per step, illustrating why the combined memory-and-operation metric matters.

For non-Born–Oppenheimer dynamics of C₂₃H₂₀N₃O, the paper reports an 8.22-fold cost reduction, from 4.98 × 10¹⁵ to 6.06 × 10¹⁴, through measurement-based cleanup of copied coordinates, a Bernstein-polynomial approximation that avoids the baseline’s multiplication step when evaluating 1/r and simpler handling of nuclear charges. For Cytochrome P450, cost fell by a factor of 2.49 while memory dropped from 481 to 333 logical qubits, principally by replacing bulky angle lookups with one-hot registers, which mark the chosen term on a dedicated qubit.

The arithmetic result combined two forms of search. The paper reports that agents first tested circuits within a restricted, classically simulable gate set, then used Lean verification to optimize beyond it, reaching 3,698 T gates on 100 qubits and reducing spacetime cost by a factor greater than 290. For parallel Grover search, where the circuits had to succeed with certainty, expected oracle rounds fell by factors of up to 1.22 when finding any target and 2.57 when finding all targets in the tested multi-target regimes.

Public Resources and Remaining Constraints

The November 23 post is the later official presentation of research already public elsewhere. The arXiv record for Discovering formally verified quantum programs with AI dates the first submission to November 6, 2026 and the third version to November 16, 2026; the manuscript is dated November 17, 2026. The official repository carries a November 17, 2026 publication commit.

The repository separates the core

QuantumComputation library from QuantumComputationSpecs, which holds specifications and benchmark challenges; discovered programs sit in its discoveries branch. It is under active development, with explicit models for costing classical computation and control flow listed as the next milestone.

DeepMind says the end-to-end simulations still demand far more resources than projected for the first fault-tolerant quantum computers and that further orders-of-magnitude reductions are needed. The results are also bounded by their specifications: the molecular-dynamics task requires correctness even on unphysical input states, while the Cytochrome P450 task fixes the tensor factorization and excludes possible representation improvements.

The immediate advance is a verified discovery process rather than a demonstration on quantum hardware: agents can propose and prove reductions beyond classical testing, while humans remain responsible for the physical model and cost conventions those proofs enforce. The practical question is how much of the reported gain remains as specifications grow to include error-correcting codes, qubit routing and physical layouts.
summary: Google DeepMind presented research on November 23, 2026 showing that teams of Gemini 4 agents, checked by the Lean theorem prover, produced lower-cost quantum programs for five problems.
